title: A Model Shows How California’s Earthquake ‘Gate’ Works
summary:
A meeting point between two California fault systems can act a little like a gate, scientists report. Sometimes an earthquake rupture stops there. Under other conditions, it can continue onto the next fault system.

A fault is a break in Earth’s crust where sections of rock can move past one another. When those sections become stuck, stress can build. An earthquake can happen when stored energy is released and the rocks move. A rupture is the breaking and movement that spreads along a fault during an earthquake.

The new study focuses on the San Andreas and San Jacinto fault systems. They come close together at Cajon Pass, northeast of Los Angeles. Researchers used a computer model to explore about 1,000 years of earthquake activity there.

The model suggests that stress in parts of the system now matches or exceeds the highest levels in its simulated history. These results are estimates from a model.

Past earthquakes show why the junction matters. In 1857, the Fort Tejon earthquake’s rupture stopped at Cajon Pass. In 1812, the Wrightwood earthquake’s rupture passed through the junction and involved both systems.

The researchers call Cajon Pass an earthquake gate because its behavior depends on changing stress conditions. It does not always block a rupture or always let one through.

The study helps scientists understand how stress builds and moves between faults over centuries.
why_it_matters: Understanding how stress changes near a fault junction helps scientists study why an earthquake rupture may stop or continue onto another fault system.
